activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20; both describe the same eyesight.
story:
The eye clinic sat between a smoothie shop and a shoe store, and Jessica had been past it a hundred times without ever once going in. Today she stood at its counter while her mother filled out forms, and Jessica stared at the chart on the far wall, squinting until the letters blurred back together. The top line said E. She was almost sure it said E.

"Jessica Vance," called a man in a white coat. His name tag read Mr. Xu. "Come on back. We'll get you sorted before your audition, don't worry."

"It's at four o'clock," Jessica said, checking her phone. "The school talent show tryouts. I'm singing." She still had two hours, but the bus took forty minutes, and lately she'd been walking right past her stop because she couldn't read the number on the sign until the bus had already pulled away. That was the whole reason she was here.

Her friend King had come along, mostly for the food court afterward, and he leaned in the doorway of the exam room. "My cousin visiting from Australia says she has six-six vision," he said. "I told her that's impossible, twenty-twenty is perfect."

Mr. Xu didn't answer. He just flipped the lens machine in front of Jessica's face and slid one dial after another. "Better or worse?" Each time, Jessica had to decide, and each time the letters sharpened or softened like the focus on a camera. It was strange, she thought, that nobody could see her eyesight except her. The optometrist could only measure it and trust what she reported.

Then it hit her. "Wait," she said. "Australia uses metres. My cousin from England says six-six too, and England uses metres." She looked at Mr. Xu. "Six-six and twenty-twenty are the same thing? Two different measuring systems, same eyes?"

"Six-six in metric countries, twenty-twenty here," Mr. Xu said with a small nod. "Both describe the same eyesight." He slid one more lens into place. "How's this?"

"Better. A lot better." The chart jumped into focus so sharply that she laughed out loud, because the second line didn't just say F, it said F P T O Z, and there was a third line, and a fourth. She could see the dust on the chart's frame. She turned to King. "Your cousin has perfect vision. She just measures it in metres."

"Told you nothing was wrong with her," King said, though he hadn't, and Jessica let it go because it didn't matter.

Choosing frames took forever. The sophisticated titanium pair looked amazing but cost more than her mother's shoes budget for the year, so Jessica adjusted the simpler wire pair on her nose in the mirror and decided they'd do. Mr. Xu promised the lenses would be cut in twenty minutes, which left just enough time for King to run to the smoothie shop and bring back a mango one, which he handed her without being asked, extra napkins tucked under the lid because he knew she always spilled.

The glasses came ready at 3:20, warm from the lab, and the whole mall snapped into detail as she slid them on: price tags, sale signs, a baby's sock dropped by the fountain. On the bus, she read her stop number from half a block away and pulled the cord in time. At the audition, she stood on stage, saw the piano keys clearly across the room, and sang.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Ms. Ricci had written two sentences on the board and asked the class to sort them: "Pickle pizza is delicious" and "Our classroom fern gets watered every Tuesday." Brooklyn copied both into her notebook, which was more than Royce was doing. Royce was drawing a shark with laser eyes.

"Obviously the pizza one is an opinion," he said before Ms. Ricci had even finished passing out the lab sheets. "And the fern thing is just, like, my opinion too. I mean, who says it's Tuesday? Time is basically a feeling."

Brooklyn looked at the fern. It sat on the windowsill between two bean seedlings the class had planted last week, and both seedlings were slumped over like they'd given up on the semester. She raised her hand anyway. "The fern thing can be checked. We could ask who waters it, or look at the schedule, or hide a camera."

"That's surveillance," Royce said. "Also my opinion."

"It's not an opinion if it can be checked," Brooklyn said. "It's a claim. Like if I said the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin. That's not my opinion. That's just wrong. I could check it, and it would be false."

Royce opened his mouth, then closed it, which for Royce was practically a scientific event. Ms. Ricci wrote the word "claim" on the board without comment and moved on to the bean seedlings, which was convenient, because Brooklyn actually cared about the beans. The seedlings in jar A were thriving. The ones in jar B were dying, and both jars sat in the same window with the same water. Something unseen was doing this.

She had a hypothetical cause: maybe the seeds in jar B had been stored near the radiator over winter, so their stored carbohydrate, the food a seed lives on before it sprouts, had been used up or ruined while the jar A seeds stayed cool. It was a guess about something she couldn't see, the inside of a seed, so it needed a test. She took four fresh seeds from each jar, laid them on wet paper towels in labeled bags, and put them in the cabinet where Ms. Ricci kept the preserve jars and the smells of vinegar that clung to everything. If the jar B seeds sprouted fine in the cabinet, her radiator idea was wrong. If they flopped again, she was onto something.

The pizza, meanwhile, had not gone away. Royce brought it up at lunch, waving a hypothetical slice he described in unnecessary detail, and Cameron, who had heard about the fern, asked Brooklyn whether liking pickle pizza could ever be false. "No," Brooklyn said. "It's just taste. It can't be checked. There's nothing to check." Cameron nodded slowly, like a man receiving bad news about a sandwich he'd already eaten.

Three days later she opened the cabinet. The jar A seeds had fat white roots curling through the paper towels. The jar B seeds had done almost nothing, one brave sprout and three shrugs. She carried both bags to Ms. Ricci's desk, and behind her Royce said, quietly, "Okay, so the tower thing. The Eiffel Tower is not in Berlin."

"Correct," Brooklyn said, and pinned the B bag to the board next to the word "claim."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
The lobby chat filled with small yellow messages while Rachel adjusted her headset. "Team Sunset Dynasty, ready to lose?" Nicholas typed, which was his way of saying good morning. Rachel grinned and queued them up, but her eyes kept drifting to the side of the screen, where her friend Soraya had just posted a photo to the team's shared board. It was a selfie on a porch, a victory pose with her new rank badge held up like a trophy. Rachel zoomed in without really thinking about it, the way she did with any screenshot, looking for detail.

The porch was nice. The railing, the welcome mat, a potted plant. And behind Soraya's smiling face, small but sharp, a house number on the door frame, and beside it a street sign at the corner of the block, just visible over the hedge. Rachel sat back. She thought about the eleven thousand players in this game's community, some of whom she had never met, and how the photo was set to public because Soraya never touched her settings. A stranger could zoom in the same way Rachel just had. A stranger could look at a house number and a street sign and work out exactly where the photo was taken. That part was simple. The part that made her stomach tighten was what came after.

She took a screenshot of her own zoom, cropped it to just the door frame and the sign, and sent it to Soraya with a single message: "Look what I can see."

The next round started without her. Nicholas's character got eliminated twice while Rachel stared at the chat window, waiting. Then Soraya's reply appeared: "What am I looking at?"

"Your house number. And your street," Rachel typed. "The photo's public. Try to find my house from this." She attached a test photo she had just taken of her own porch, but this time she had angled herself against the blank garage door, nothing behind her but smooth gray. If Soraya could find Rachel's house from that, Rachel would stop worrying. If she couldn't, the worry was worth something.

Soraya spent six minutes trying. She asked for the town, and Rachel gave it, being as impartial as a referee, offering no hints either way. Soraya found nothing. No number, no sign, no school logo on a hoodie, nothing. "Okay, you win," she finally typed. "Deleting the porch one. Should I retake it in front of the garage like yours?"

"Or the fence," Nicholas cut in, having clearly been reading the whole time. "The fence is very dramatic. Very mysterious. Like a dynasty that fell because everyone could see its address." Rachel laughed out loud, and in the lobby two teammates asked what was so funny.

Soraya posted the new photo an hour later, taken against the fence, and beneath it she wrote that she had gone into her settings and turned the board to friends-only besides. Then she sent Rachel a private message: "There are four other people on the team with porch photos. Want to help me check them?"

Rachel exhaled, sat up straighter, and opened the board. One by one, zoom by zoom, she and Soraya messaged each teammate, and by the end of the evening every background had been checked and two more photos had been retaken. Ms. Sok, whose nephew apparently played on their team under the name FalconGirl88, sent a message too: "Nice work, team. Falcon's photo was all fence before I even asked."

"We run a tight dynasty," Nicholas announced in the lobby.

"A mysterious one," Rachel said, and started the next round.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly, was first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert.
story:
Chloe pushed her chair in at the family dinner table and slid a folded paper across to her dad. "Guess what happened at the garden club today."

"You finally got the marigolds planted?" her mom asked, passing the potatoes.

"Better. I fixed the meetings." Chloe unfolded the paper, which had AGENDA written across the top in her careful handwriting. "Every meeting we've ever had turns into Milena and Ronald arguing about fundraisers while everybody else just sits there. Last week, Mr. Mwangi came to advise us and he couldn't even get a word in. I figured there had to be a reason meetings kept going like that, some kind of pattern, and I wanted to find the rule underneath it."

Her dad raised an eyebrow. "And you found this rule where?"

"The library shelf behind the bake sale box. There's this old book, dusty, falling apart. It's called Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly. It was first published in 1876 by a U.S. Army officer named Henry Martyn Robert. An army officer, Dad. Writing meeting rules."

"Soldiers have meetings too," her dad said, grinning.

"Anyway," Chloe said, waving her fork, "I read half of it last night. It's actually kind of sophisticated. You keep a list, an agenda, and people raise hands, and nobody talks over anybody. So today I budgeted exactly ten minutes per topic, and I ran the whole meeting with the book right next to me like a referee."

Her little brother snorted. "Did Ronald follow the rules?"

"That's the best part. He tried to interrupt Milena about the car wash, and I said, 'Ronald, you're on the list for after her.' And he actually sat back down. He looked a little shocked, like the chairs themselves had spoken." Chloe laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her milk. "Then Milena finished her point in two minutes because nobody was racing her, and this quiet kid who never talks suggested we sell herb seed packets, and everybody loved it. We voted and everything. A real vote, with hands."

"So the old book worked," her mom said.

"It worked because it's fair, that's the thing," Chloe said. "It's not me being bossy. The rules don't care who's loudest. I have this ambition now, this plan. Next meeting, I'm teaching everyone else the basics so the club keeps running this way even when I'm not president anymore." She refolded the paper and tucked it into her back pocket.

"Chloe," her dad said, "you just made an 1876 army officer the hero of the garden club."

She stood up and grabbed the old book from her chair. "He's not the hero. He's the coach." Then she was already halfway to the stairs, calling over her shoulder, "Meeting notes to write!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
The screen above the counter filled half the wall of Marconi's, and every seat in the place faced it. Lucy slid into the booth between Ella and Alina, her dad on the outside with a basket of garlic knots, and on the screen the Comets were ten minutes from finishing the championship game.

"Say it now," Ella said, "so I can enjoy it. Comets win because they're the better team."

Alina looked skeptical. "They've played every playoff game at home. Put them on a neutral field and I'm not sure."

"That's such an excuse," Ella said.

Lucy chewed a garlic knot and thought about last spring, when she'd insisted her debate team only lost because the judges were unfair. Later she'd found the recordings and heard her own stumbling opening. She had never said that out loud to anyone, and it still sat wrong with her.

"They do seem different at home," Lucy said slowly. "But is that a real thing or just a story people tell?"

"Look it up," Alina said, mouth full of pizza.

Lucy pulled out her phone under the table, careful of Ms. Nguyen, whose booth was across the aisle. Ms. Nguyen taught science at their school and had once confiscated Alina's phone for a week. Lucy typed fast. Then she read it twice.

"Okay, this is real," she said. "In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games. It even has a name. Home advantage."

"Ha," Alina said, not even pretending to be quiet.

"But wait," Lucy said. She turned the phone so Ella could see. "More than half isn't all of it. It's a tilt, not a wall. The Comets could still be better."

Ella sat back. "So the truth is annoying. Both things at once."

On the screen the Comets' striker took a ball off a defender's foot, cut inside, and buried it in the far corner. The restaurant erupted. Lucy's dad knocked over the parmesan shaker trying to high-five Ella, and a waiter came jogging over with a stack of napkins like he was responding to a plumbing emergency.

"Sorry, sorry," her dad said, mopping.

Ella reached over and consoled the shaker, patting its top. "It's okay, buddy."

Lucy was still holding her phone, scrolling. Some teams showed bigger home advantages than others, season to season, and none of it settled whether this team, tonight, deserved it. She closed the phone and put it face down.

"Here's what I think," she said. "They were good at home all season. That counts. But next year, first away game, I want to watch."

Alina raised her soda. "To away games."

"To evidence," Ella said, and clinked her cup against it.

From the next booth, Ms. Nguyen leaned over without looking up from her salad and said, "For what it's worth, that's the best sentence I've heard all year."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
story:
Alex had texted Zackery three times before the Tomas family's kitchen light finally felt less scary: I'm babysitting, what if she cries, what if I ruin everything? Zackery's last reply still glowed on the screen: "You'll figure it out. You always do." Two-year-old Mia banged a plastic spoon on the high chair tray and grinned at him, and Alex decided that maybe Zackery was right.

He had made a systematic plan, written on a napkin and taped above the sink: snack at six, blocks at six thirty, bath at seven, bed at seven thirty. He was proud of the napkin. He followed it exactly. He had not planned for what happened at 6:42, when he turned to rinse the snack bowl and heard a cupboard door click open behind him.

Mia stood by the counter holding the spray bottle of surface cleaner, and the trigger was loose in her fist, and there was a wet stripe down her chin. Alex's whole body went cold. He took the bottle gently out of her hands, kept his voice light, and set her on the high chair where he could see her. Then he crouched and studied the label, but the tiny print swam in front of him. For one second despair pressed down on him, and he almost called his mom at work, but she was two towns away and Mia was right here, with something on her face that might be cleaner or might be just drool.

Then he remembered the fridge. Down at the bottom, under a cartoon magnet, hung a strip of paper with numbers on it. He peeled it off. At the top, in the mother's handwriting, it said POISON HELP, and under that: 1-800-222-1222. Alex grabbed his phone and dialed. A woman answered before the second ring finished.

"Hi, my name is Alex, I'm babysitting, and a toddler got hold of a cleaner bottle," he said. "I don't know if she swallowed any."

"You did exactly the right thing calling," the woman said. "This number, 1-800-222-1222, is the Poison Help line, and it connects you to your local poison control center at any hour, even right now." She asked what the bottle said, whether Mia was coughing, whether she was acting normal. Alex read the label out loud, letter by letter, while Mia chewed the spoon and watched him. The woman told him what to watch for and said to call back any time, for any reason, even if he just felt unsure. He said thank you twice.

Mia went to bed at 7:30 exactly, right on schedule. Alex sat at the kitchen table and texted Zackery: "I handled it." Then he took the napkin plan off the wall, smoothed it flat, and wrote one more line at the bottom, 1-800-222-1222, and taped it up where he would never miss it.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.
story:
Piper stood at the bathroom sink with her flashcards propped against the mirror, rehearsing her health presentation for the fourth time. On Monday she had to explain, in two minutes, how nicotine hooks the brain, and Mr. Hughes had said her first attempt sounded like she was reading a dictionary. Behind her, water dripped from the faucet with a steady plink.

Her uncle had given her the best material without meaning to. At his doctor's appointment last week, he had asked why he reached for a cigarette the second he got stressed, and the doctor had answered that when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about ten seconds. Piper had written it on an index card in red pen. Ten seconds. She scrutinized the card, turning it over, looking for what made it important. It was fast. Faster than almost anything else. But why did fast matter?

She tried out an answer in the mirror. "Your brain learns by connecting." Her voice bounced off the tile. She turned on the tap and let cold water run over her wrists, which is what she did before quizzes. "If something bad happens and you feel better almost right away, your brain links them. If the gap is ten seconds, the link is tight."

A knock rattled the door. "Piper, some of us need the bathroom," her brother called.

"One minute." She flicked the water off. Her idea still needed a test. She grabbed her phone and set a timer for ten seconds, then started it and stood still, counting the drips from the faucet. Four. Five. Six. Ten seconds was nothing. If her uncle felt relief within that window, his brain would barely have room to notice anything else that might have helped, like walking outside or taking a breath. The cigarette always got the credit.

She flipped through her cards to the part about dopamine and the reward pathway, which she had copied from a site her school library listed as a prestigious research institute. Then she found her facts about money, because Mr. Hughes liked presentations that answered "so what." Cigarette sales produced billions in revenue for tobacco companies every year, and those companies counted on brains that had learned, in ten seconds, to want more.

At the door she heard her brother again, and behind him Ibraheem's voice, who had come over to time her run-throughs. "Tell her Jason says even his mom quit and she's the most stubborn person alive," Ibraheem said. Piper opened the door with the cards fanned out like a poker hand.

"Ibraheem, sit on the tub," she said. "You're my class. Question one. Somebody hands you a cigarette and says one won't hurt. You have ten seconds. Go."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
story:
Jan scooped a hole in the sand and set a beach ball in it, standing upright. "Okay, Miss Science Fair. Explain the seasons again, but this time so I actually believe you."

Sarah crouched beside the ball and stuck a wooden skewer through it at an angle, like a lamppost leaning in the wind. "The Earth is tilted," she said. "Not toward the sun all the time, just sometimes. When our half leans in, summer. When it leans away, winter." She remembered the day she'd gotten this wrong, back in September, when she'd told the whole class that the Earth must swing closer to the sun in June. Ms. Sinclair had only raised an eyebrow and said, "Then why is it winter in Australia right now?" Sarah had gone home red-faced and spent two evenings with a flashlight and a grapefruit until the pattern finally turned over in her mind. She had come to cherish that grapefruit, dented as it was.

Jan spun the ball slowly, watching the skewer's shadow crawl across the sand. "Here's my problem," Jan said. "My grandmother lives near the equator. Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little. She laughs when I talk about four seasons. Her town has wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones. Winter coats, snowmen, none of it. She says a cold day there means she wears a long-sleeved shirt."

Sarah stopped with her hand on the ball. That had never come up in any of her books. She pictured the tilted skewer again, tilting toward the sun, away, toward, away, and then she imagined standing right where the skewer pointed, straight under the flashlight beam no matter how the ball leaned. "Then it works," she said slowly. "If the light barely changes all year, the temperature wouldn't either. So it isn't that her seasons are wrong. They're just driven by rain instead of warmth."

"So who's right, you or your grandmother?" Jan asked.

"Both. Maybe neither of us is the whole story." Sarah judged herself fairly, like an impartial referee between her grapefruit and Jan's grandmother, and had to admit the verdict might be a tie. She picked up the skewer and tilted the ball toward the imaginary sun. "Say the sun is that lifeguard chair. Stand on the equator line I drew and tell me what you notice about your shadow."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18.
story:
Brooke stood at the kitchen counter at ten thirty on Tuesday night, staring at the math worksheet she had barely started. Her heart was doing a fast, shallow drumroll, and her shoulders were up near her ears. She had snapped at her mom at dinner over nothing, and she could still feel a low simmer of resentment about it, which was unfair, since the snapping had been hers.

Her phone buzzed. Anastasia, from across the street: "You up? Science test still."

"Still," Brooke typed back. "Can't focus. Heart racing. Weird."

"Same last week. My cousin made me count my sleep. Try it."

Brooke pulled out a notepad. She had gone to bed at midnight, waking at six thirty for school. She counted on her fingers: six and a half hours. She counted the last three nights, and they were all about the same. She wrote the number down and stared at it, because it looked wrong, like something had been quietly taking a cut of her nights. She had assumed she was tired because of the test. Now she wondered whether the test was going badly because of the tiredness, and the idea felt like finding a leak under a sink.

A second text arrived, this one from Maxton, the twelve-year-old next door whose kitchen window faced hers. He was up gaming, his screen glowing blue across the yard. "Why are your lights on," he asked when she waved him over by phone.

"Doing sleep math," she said when he came to the back door. "I get six and a half hours. Teenagers are supposed to get eight to ten."

He frowned. "How much for kids?"

"Nine to twelve if you're six to twelve," she said. "I read the whole chart during dinner."

Maxton leaned on the counter and did his own arithmetic out loud. Midnight to seven, for a week. "That's way under nine," he said, and shut his game off without being told, which Brooke found unexpectedly eloquent, a whole argument in one click.

"Sit down," she said. "Before bed, you're supposed to breathe slow. Four counts in, hold, six out." She set the kitchen timer and did it with him, both of them at the table, the worksheet pushed aside. Her drumroll heart slowed, beat by beat, like something settling.

That night Brooke plugged her phone in downstairs, set her alarm for ten, and put a note on her pillow: test tomorrow, brain tonight. She counted the hours until morning and got nine and a half.

At breakfast the next day, her mom slid eggs onto her plate. Brooke smiled first, before anything could go wrong, and said, "Sorry about yesterday. I figured out what it was."

"What was it?"

Brooke held up nine and a half fingers. "Bedtime. Nine fifteen tonight, deal?"

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of pencil shavings and old carpet, and Nathaniel had been staring at x + 7 = 12 for four whole minutes. Across the table, Aurelie was already on problem six, her pencil whispering along like she'd been born knowing this stuff.

"How are you doing that so fast?" he asked.

"Doing what?" She didn't look up.

"The letter thing. It's a letter, Aurelie. Since when do letters equal numbers?"

She tapped his page with her eraser. "It's a mystery number. Something plus seven gives you twelve."

Nathaniel slumped back. He'd skipped breakfast to get here on time, and now his stomach was staging a small rebellion against the whole morning. Outside the window, Mr. Fitzgerald's garden looked lush and green in the June heat, which only reminded him that everyone else in the world was outside.

"Five," Aurelie said.

"I don't want the answer. I want to know how."

She finally looked at him. "You know how you got 12 in the first place? You'd take the mystery number and add seven. So think backwards."

Nathaniel wrote the equation again. He thought about his locker combination at school, how he'd once locked his gym shoes inside and the janitor had to undo the lock, turning it back the way it came. The lock had gotten to that state by turning forward, so turning backward got it out.

"Subtraction," he said slowly. "Subtraction undoes addition. So if seven got added, I can take seven away."

"From both sides," Aurelie said. "It has to stay balanced, like a seesaw. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other."

He wrote x + 7 = 12, then minus 7 under both sides. On the left, the sevens cancelled each other. On the right, 12 minus 7 was 5. x = 5. He checked it: 5 plus 7 really was 12.

"Wait," he said. "Does this work for everything? What if it's multiplication?"

Aurelie pushed her sheet toward him. "Try 3x = 15."

He stared at it. Three times something is fifteen. So something got multiplied by three, and to undo multiplication you'd divide. He wrote it out, dividing both sides by three, and there it was: x = 5 again. He laughed out loud, too loud for the quiet room, and a kid two tables over shushed him.

"Sorry," Nathaniel whispered, grinning. "It's just, I skipped toast for this."

"Sustain yourself on algebra," Aurelie said, deadpan, and went back to problem seven.

Nathaniel flipped to the next page, where the equations got longer and stranger, and squared his shoulders over problem one.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Vincent had claimed the corner of the garage behind the bicycles, where an old workbench held nine bean plants in paper cups. Each cup had a strip of masking tape with a letter on it, A through I, and a notebook lay open beside them with two weeks of measurements inside. His science fair project was supposed to answer one question: which of three fertilizers made beans grow fastest? The trouble was that his results made no sense at all. Plants A, B, and C had the blue fertilizer and had grown an average of four centimeters. Plants D, E, and F had the pink one and grown almost the same. G, H, and I had the green powder, and they had barely grown at all.

Aditya crouched beside the cups on Saturday morning, reading the notebook over Vincent's shoulder. "They're all basically the same," he said. "Except the green ones, which stink."

"That's the problem," Vincent said. "If all three fertilizers give the same result, my project is a poster that says nothing." He picked up cup B and turned it toward the window light. The stem was pale and leaning hard toward the glass.

Megane arrived with her skateboard under her arm and stopped in the doorway. She looked at the cups, then at the notebook, then at the watering can on the floor. "Wait," she said. "Which ones just get plain water?"

Vincent blinked. "None of them. They all get something."

Megane set her skateboard against the wall. "In my sister's project she had a control group," she said. "It gets no change at all, so you have something to compare against."

Vincent sat down on an upturned milk crate and stared at the cups. If every plant got fertilizer, then he could never tell whether the fertilizer was doing anything, because he had nothing to compare it with. Maybe beans grew four centimeters in two weeks no matter what. He thought about the seed packets in the drawer, the ones Ms. Leblanc had handed out in class, still sealed. He could start three more cups today with only plain water and call them his control group. The fair was in twelve days, which was tight, but beans sprouted fast in the warm garage, especially in the tropical heat that pooled near the window every afternoon. A late start might still show a difference if he checked them every morning and let the warmth accelerate the sprouting.

He filled three new cups with soil, pressed a seed into each, and watered them from the tap. Then he wrote "control" on their tape strips and started a fresh page in the notebook.

By the morning of the fair, the control plants had grown five centimeters, taller than every fertilized plant on the bench. Vincent propped his poster beside the cups, titled "Which Fertilizer Wins? None of Them." Ms. Leblanc stopped at his table, read the chart twice, and smiled.

Aditya leaned in and whispered, "So the best fertilizer is water?"

"Cheaper, too," Vincent said, and straightened the tallest control cup so everyone could see it.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
story:
The poster hung beside the trophy case outside the gym, where Justin stopped every day on his way to math. It showed a smiling man holding a piggy bank, and beneath him two numbers: an interest rate of 3.90 percent and, in smaller type, an APY of 3.98 percent. Justin had walked past it for two weeks without noticing. Today he stopped, because Ms. Shevchenko had just assigned a project on saving money over five years, and he had nothing yet.

He found Emile and Callan at the long table by the library windows. Callan was consuming a bag of pretzels so fast that crumbs dotted his history homework. "Look at this," Justin said, holding up his phone, where he'd snapped a picture of the poster. "Same bank, same account, two different rates. One of them has to be wrong, right?"

Callan leaned in, chewing. Emile pulled out a pencil and copied both numbers onto the margin of his notebook. "Maybe it's a typo," Callan said. "Banks make typos." But Justin doubted it. A bank that could afford a poster that size could afford to check two numbers, and the poster looked diligent about everything else, right down to the fine print. "There's a word here," he said. "APY. I've seen it at my dad's bank too, always a little higher than the rate."

Emile squinted at the small letters at the bottom of the picture. "It says something about a law. Truth in Savings Act of 1991." He read it aloud twice. "It says banks in the United States have to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield." "An annual percentage yield," Justin repeated, writing it down. "The APY. So they're not allowed to just show the plain rate. It includes compounding, whatever that means."

They tested it right there. Justin imagined a hundred dollars in the account, and Emile worked the plain rate first, 3.90 percent, year after year for five years. Then Callan, who had finally stopped eating, tried the APY of 3.98 percent the same way. The second pile ended up bigger, though not by a fortune. "So the APY is the honest number," Justin said slowly. "The other one's smaller because it leaves something out. The law makes them show the bigger one so nobody gets fooled." It felt like finding a hidden rule that had been posted on the wall the whole time.

Ms. Shevchenko passed their table on her way to the printer. "You three have been at this for forty minutes," she said. "More stamina than you show in gym, Callan." She glanced at their margins, crowded with numbers, and at Justin's phone still open to the poster. She didn't say anything else, which Justin took as a good sign.

He still had to build the five-year chart for Monday, column by column, plain rate beside APY, so the difference showed up on the page. His grandfather had promised him a hundred dollars if he mowed the lawn all summer, and suddenly the account in the poster seemed like a real place that money could go. He borrowed a library pencil, opened a fresh page, and wrote "Year 1" at the top.

Callan looked over his shoulder. "Which number are you using?" Justin tapped the APY twice with the eraser end. "The one the law likes."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
Adam typed the joke fast, before he could lose his nerve. "Our class project is so good we should submit it to the principal as a hostage situation." He hit enter in the school computer lab chat, where Ms. Rosen had asked everyone to post feedback on the group presentation.

Liv replied first. "Adam, that's not funny. We could actually get in trouble for that." Three other classmates typed careful, neutral replies about maybe softening the wording. Adam winced and scrolled up and down, looking for some way to take it back. It was a joke, obviously a joke, but the screen gave nothing away. Words just sat there, flat.

He leaned over to Asiya's monitor. "Can they tell I'm kidding?"

She read the thread and winced too. "Not even slightly. Tone doesn't travel."

Adam opened a new tab and searched how to show you are joking in text. The first result stopped him cold. A computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. He read it twice. Someone had invented the smiley face for exactly his problem, decades before he was born, and the reason was printed right there in one line.

"That's it," he said. "That's the whole thing. Somebody made this on purpose."

Liv slid her chair over, arms crossed, skepticism all over her face. "So you're going to fix a bad joke by sticking an emoji on it?"

"A classic," Adam said. "The original. Fahlman used a colon and a parenthesis."

He retyped his post: "Our class project is so good we should submit it to the principal as a hostage situation :-)". Then he waited, watching the chat like a fisherman watching a bobber. Ms. Rosen crossed the room, stopped behind their row, and read the screen. The class went quiet in that way it does when everyone expects trouble.

She tilted her head. "Better," she said. "The first version could have been read literally, and this one can't. That's the entire history of the problem, solved with two keystrokes." She tapped the top of Liv's monitor. "Liv, good catch on the tone. Adam, good fix. Now everyone, actual feedback on the presentation, and you may use any punctuation you find necessary."

Asiya grinned and typed fast. Her post appeared in the chat: "I liked slide three :-)".

Liv rolled her eyes, but she was smiling as she typed back, "Fine. Slide three was good :-)."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: The old <center> tag was deprecated in HTML 4 in favour of the CSS text-align property.
story:
Hunter slid into the seat beside Braylon at the library's computer table and pulled a folded printout from his backpack. It was an old web tutorial his grandpa had mailed him, six yellowed pages about building a first web page, with a note clipped to the front.

"Dear Hunter," Braylon read over his shoulder, grinning. "Your grandmother says I built our bakery's site in 1999, which makes me a professional. Ignore the part about dial-up. Love, Grandpa."

"You get one guess about whether I'm building this," Hunter said. He wanted a real site for their class book-review club, with a big centred heading across the top, and he wanted it done before Saturday so Braylon could show it to his cousin, who had promised, in writing, to "make a better one in ten minutes." Braylon took that as a challenge. Hunter took it as a deadline.

He typed the tutorial's heading line exactly, with the tag it said to use, center, wrapped right around the words. He saved the file, opened it in the browser, and the heading sat stubbornly on the left. He typed it again, slower, as if the computer might be more obedient the second time. Still left. The library printer gave an abrupt clunk behind them and Jai appeared with a page about computer viruses, which she needed for her homework on how they spread. "One virus and I'll scream," she said, dropping into the third chair. "Mine's on paper."

Hunter stared at the screen. The tag had to be the problem, because everything else on the page worked, and a thing that works in one spot but not another usually means the difference is the thing you changed. He had a theory: maybe the tutorial was too old, and the browser simply didn't listen to that tag anymore. "That tag is like a virus," Braylon said, "spreading through your whole tutorial." He flipped pages and found it three more times. Instead of trusting it, Hunter opened the library's search box, typed the tag's name, and scrolled until he found the answer: the center tag was deprecated in HTML 4 in favour of the CSS text-align property. He read the line twice.

"Deprecated," he said out loud. "It means retired." He revised the heading, deleted the old tag, and wrote style equals text-align colon center into the heading itself, following the example. He saved, held his breath, and refreshed.

The heading glided to the middle of the page like it had always wanted to be there. Braylon punched the air. Jai leaned over to look, then pointed at the screen. "Can you make mine a web page too? Just a title that says, Do Not Click Suspicious Links."

Hunter cracked his knuckles. "One centred heading, coming up."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important.
story:
Alexis sat on the floor of Casey's basement with his laptop balanced on a cardboard box, because the beanbag had swallowed the extension cord. The contest page had to be submitted by nine o'clock tonight, and it was already six. His page was about a tropical trip his family had taken to Kauai, and it had exactly one requirement from Ms. Mehta: a proper title, centred, at the top.

"That's the title?" Javier asked, leaning over. On the screen, the words "My Kauai Journal" sat in the top left corner, small and gray, looking about as important as a grocery list.

Alexis had typed the title inside a heading tag, but he'd used h3, because he'd copied a line from somewhere and never thought about it. He tried centring it first. He added text-align: center to his CSS rule, and the little gray words slid to the middle of the page. Centred, yes. Still tiny.

"The title's supposed to be the big one," Casey said from the couch, where he was reading the contest rules on his phone. "Ms. Mehta posted an example."

She had also posted a message to the whole class at five o'clock, and Casey read it out loud: "Reminder: no site builders that generate the page for you. Everyone writes the HTML by hand. Contest closes at nine. Anyone still guessing at tags, remember that HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, and h1 is the most important."

Alexis read the message twice. Six levels. So the numbers weren't random decorations; they were a rank. If h3 was small, h1 had to be the top of the scale. He changed the tag to h1, saved, and refreshed the browser. "My Kauai Journal" appeared large and black, still sitting dead center from the CSS he'd already written.

"Try h6 too," Javier said. "Just to check the pattern."

Alexis swapped in h6, and the title shrank to almost nothing. He changed it back to h1 and left it. The pattern held all the way down, which meant he could use h2 for the section called "Snorkeling at Tunnels Beach" and h3 for "What the eel did," and the page would organize itself by importance, exactly like an outline.

At eight forty, Casey's phone buzzed with one last message from Ms. Mehta: "Ten minutes of my evening to remind you all that hand-checking your own code is a privilege I did not have at your age." Alexis attached his file and hit submit at eight fifty-two. On the screen, the big centred title loaded, and under it, in order, the beach, the eel, and a photo of a gecko on the rental car.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: The old <center> tag was deprecated in HTML 4 in favour of the CSS text-align property.
story:
Alexa had exactly one hour before the library closed, and one goal: get the big heading on her web page to sit in the middle of the screen instead of sulking in the corner like a cat that had been told "no." She and Isa had signed up for the school's website contest, and Isa had already built a page about axolotls with three pictures and a joke section. Alexa's page, on the other hand, had a heading shoved against the left edge as if it were trying to hibernate there until spring.

Ms. Fortin, the librarian, had set her up at the computer by the window, where the afternoon sun warmed the keyboard and everything smelled like old paper and floor wax. Alexa was working from a tutorial her grandpa had printed out years ago, a stack of pages held together with a binder clip. "Make a heading centered," it said, and then it showed her a tag that said center, spelled out in angle brackets. Alexa typed it exactly the way the paper showed, wrapping it around her heading, and hit refresh.

Nothing happened. The heading stayed exactly where it was, still against the left edge, still apparently in a bad mood. She retyped it. Still nothing. She checked for typos three times, once with her finger on the screen, which Isa always said was like poking the problem to see if it would confess.

Fionn appeared behind her with a book about bridges under one arm, peering over her shoulder. "Why is your title hiding in the corner?"

"It's not hiding, it's broken," Alexa said. Then she stopped. She squinted at her grandpa's printed pages, and at the library's big book of current web standards on the shelf beside the computer, which Ms. Fortin had left there after a colleague recommended it. She flipped to the index and ran her finger down the page. There it was, plain as anything: the old center tag had been deprecated in HTML 4, and the book said to use the CSS text-align property instead. "Deprecated," Fionn read aloud. "That's a fancy word for retired."

"Grandpa's tutorial is older than HTML 4," Alexa said, laughing. She deleted the old tag, found the CSS section, and typed a rule that set text-align to center. She held her breath and pressed refresh, and the heading slid to the middle of the screen like it had been waiting all along for someone to ask politely.

Isa wandered over, looked at the page, and frowned. "Shouldn't it be a little more to the left? Perfectly centered looks off to me."

"That's subjective," Alexa said. "Also, you're wrong." Ms. Fortin passed by their table, glanced at the screen, and gave a small nod of approval before wheeling her cart of returns toward the biography section. Alexa saved her file twice, because contests had rules and paranoia had its uses, and then turned the keyboard toward Isa. "Your turn. Type your axolotl joke exactly as I showed you."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Hailey kept her hand on the rail of the wide marble staircase as their class climbed toward courtroom three. Ms. Islam had distributed the pamphlets on the bus, one per student, and Hailey had read hers twice already. At the top of the stairs, while the others wandered toward the tall doors, she read it a third time and felt the same snag she'd felt the first time. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section one. Guarantee of rights and freedoms. It began with guarantees, with lists, and something about the opening bothered her, the way a word on the tip of your tongue bothers you.

"Read me yours," Mariah said, bumping her shoulder. "Mine's all smudged."

Hailey read the opening aloud in a low voice. "What kind of word starts a whole country's most important document?" she asked. "Ours starts with guarantees. What does Germany's start with? My cousins live there, and their mom says their constitution has a name."

"Germany has a constitution?" Santiago said, joining them. "I thought that was, like, an American thing."

"My aunt calls it the Basic Law," Hailey said. "That's the name for it there."

Ms. Islam clapped her hands then, and they filed into the courtroom, where a clerk was stacking binders and the afternoon light came through windows so tall they seemed extravagant for a room that was mostly wood and silence. The judge, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, invited them to sit. Then she said something that made Hailey sit up straight. "Before we hear any case in this room," the judge said, "we remember that the law exists for one reason. In Germany, after the war, they rebuilt their whole legal system, and they put it in writing in 1949. That document is called the Basic Law, and its very first article begins, 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'"

Hailey's pencil was out before the judge finished. Not guarantees, she thought. Not lists. Dignity first, before everything else. She tried the idea the way you test a bridge by stepping on it. If dignity comes first, then all the other rights might just be ways of protecting that one thing. Like how the rights in her pamphlet, freedom of expression, protection from unfair search, were all fingers of the same hand.

When the judge asked for questions, Hailey's hand rose before she decided to raise it. "Could I try to say Article 1 in my own words?" she asked. "For my assignment?"

The judge took off her glasses. "Go ahead."

"It means nobody can ever touch the part of you that makes you a person," Hailey said slowly, feeling her way. "Not the government, not a judge, not anyone. It can't be broken. That's why they wrote it down first, in 1949, so everyone would know where to start." She thought of the smudged pamphlet in Mariah's pocket, of how ink on paper could hold a promise you couldn't see, the way soil holds the work of decomposers you never watch, and how something built out of sight still feeds everything that grows after it.

"Better than most law students," the judge said, and put her glasses back on. "Court is now in session."
